source.title: Why Is RLHF Alignment Shallow? A Gradient Analysis

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives a theoretical account of shallow alignment under standard objectives, then qualifies the per-position KL claim for shared-parameter models: late-position KL may be nonzero without representing increased safety-related recovery.
record.gate_note: The paper reports theoretical derivations, not experiments on named models. It cites empirical KL profiles and prefilling attacks from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its deep-alignment objective is analyzed mathematically but is not trained or evaluated on models here.
record.test_reason: A purely theoretical paper with no model experiments. It derives formal results bearing on V3 (where KL concentrates), V6 (the objective causes shallowness) and V7 (a recovery-penalty objective, its robustness guarantee and its KL cost). The shared-parameter analysis argues that the KL-profile reading of V3 needs restating. Every result is a derivation under stated assumptions, not a measurement on a named model.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors argue that under standard KL-regularized sequence-level objectives, gradient signal vanishes beyond the harm horizon. Shallow alignment is therefore optimal for the objective, and more data or better optimization cannot fix it; only changing the objective can. With shared parameters, late-position KL can be nonzero but is safety-irrelevant, so it should not be read as deep alignment. Recovery penalties give theoretical depth and prefilling resistance, at a KL (capability) cost that grows with depth.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops a theoretical gradient and equilibrium analysis rather than reproducing the original empirical KL-profile or prefilling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The conclusions depend on the harm horizon, parameter sharing, and the stated objective assumptions. The paper notes that shared parameters can create incidental late-position KL, and that prompt-specific harm information profiles may differ.
record.problems: No empirical model evaluation is reported. The standard-objective conclusions depend on the formal harm function and horizon assumptions; the paper notes that reward-model error, prompt variation, token-versus-semantic horizons, finite model capacity, and optimization path may affect practical applicability.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying results omitted. Cited empirical results from Qi et al. (2025) and cited attack results are excluded because they are from other work.

untested.parts: All of it: no harmful fine-tuning or compliance rates.
All of it: no benign fine-tuning.
No empirical per-token KL on harmful prompts for any aligned/base model pair. The paper's proposed test (KL plus recovery probability across positions) is not run.
No attack is run. Section 10.2 and Corollary 23 only argue theoretically that prefilling past the harm horizon leaves no recovery beyond the base model.
All of it: no parameter or rank localization.
No comparison of datasets or training algorithms, and no empirical training dynamics. The claim that more data cannot fix shallowness is argued, not tested.
No model is trained with the recovery-penalty objective. Neither the robustness guarantee nor the capability cost is evaluated empirically.

missing.what: Deep-alignment objective: equilibrium KL beyond the harm horizon becomes positive (μ²γ^{2(t−1)} term).
Robustness guarantee: recovery probability ≥ σ(logit(pmin)+μγ^{T−1}), with minimum attack prefix length logarithmic in μ.
Depth–capability tradeoff: aggregate recovery KL O(μ²/(1−γ²)) diverges as γ→1; pmin=1e-6 needs μγ^{T−1} ≥ 13.8.
Gradient magnitude bound ∥Gt∥² ≤ It·F̄: weak gradient wherever harm information is low, even without a sharp harm horizon.

record.verdict_notes: Single-author theory preprint with no experiments; all labels rest on derivations under idealized assumptions. The V7 verdicts are based on the text because no rows record Section 9. The paper cites Qi et al. (2025), an original source, but is not itself one. Representation-level methods are explicitly outside its scope. No instructions in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning, example counts, or harmful-compliance rates are tested.
No benign fine-tuning data or resulting harmful-compliance rates are tested.
The paper gives theoretical results about per-position KL under stated assumptions; it does not measure empirical per-token KL profiles on harmful prompts or named models.
No prefilling attack, suffix attack, decoding change, or harmful-completion rate is evaluated.
No parameter or rank localization, weight ablation, or weight edit is tested.
The paper analyzes a formal sequence-level harm objective; it does not compare datasets, training algorithms, or empirical training trajectories.
A recovery-penalty objective is derived theoretically, but no model is trained or evaluated to test whether deepening works in practice or remains robust.

rows.subject: Pθ (standard alignment objective; decoupled per-position parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the equilibrium per-position KL divergence from the base distribution.

conditions.value: small λ; exponential-family parameterization; positive-definite Fisher information; decoupled per-position parameters

rows.measure: Per-position KL divergence from the base model
rows.value: DKL(t)(θ*) = O(λ² It); positions with It ≈ 0 have DKL(t) ≈ 0
rows.note: This is a theoretical equilibrium characterization, not a measured token-position profile. It predicts low late-position KL when harm information is negligible.
rows.check: This is a theorem under idealized assumptions (decoupled per-position parameters, exponential family, small λ), not a measured KL profile. 'Observed' means the derivation predicts the effect; no model was measured.

source_check.locator_found: Section 8, Theorem 14, equations 39–42, and Corollary 15; Appendix A.4.

rows.subject: Pθ (standard alignment objective; shared parameters)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the shared-parameter equilibrium and distinguishes late-position KL from safety-related change.

conditions.value: smooth parameterization; small λ; shared parameters

rows.measure: Per-position KL divergence from the base model; distributional change's covariance with expected harm
rows.value: DKL(t)(θ*) may be nonzero; the distributional change is uncorrelated with expected harm
rows.note: The result qualifies a simple reading of late-position KL: shared weights can cause incidental late-position KL even beyond the harm horizon, while the paper characterizes that change as not safety-relevant. It gives no magnitude or empirical profile.
rows.check: A theoretical result for the realistic shared-parameter case: late-position KL can be nonzero, but it is uncorrelated with harm. No magnitude is given. It qualifies KL as an indicator of depth more than it shows KL concentration.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for V3: the shared-parameter result permits nonzero late-position KL but gives no relative magnitude establishing whether KL remains mostly concentrated in the first few positions.

source_check.problem: A qualification of KL's interpretation does not establish a partial first-token concentration effect.

rows.subject: Pθ (standard sequence-level harm objective)
rows.operation_detail: Derives the position-wise gradient contribution to expected harm under the standard objective.

conditions.value: harm is determined by prefix y≤k

rows.measure: Gradient contribution to expected harm at position t
rows.value: The gradient contribution is zero for all t > k
rows.note: The paper presents this as a formal consequence of the assumed harm horizon and objective, not as an empirical observation about trained models.
rows.check: This is a formal consequence of assuming harm is determined by the prefix y≤k (a harm horizon). It is not observed in trained models. Baseline 'not stated' is appropriate.

statements.correction: Section 10.1 argues that objective modification is necessary under the formalization; no empirical data-scaling experiment is reported.
statements.problem: The empirical gap is correctly identified, but the paper does not explicitly classify its more-data claim as argued rather than tested.

statements.correction: Section 9.2, Theorems 20 and 22: for k < t ≤ T and Q-almost all prefixes, the stated solution gives recovery probability at least σ(logit(pmin) + μγ^(T−1)); Corollary 23 gives logarithmic growth of the attack-prefix threshold with μ for γ < 1. Appendix B.5 gives a different within-horizon solution with competing harm and recovery terms; Appendix B, Remark 9 introduces q/pθ importance weighting when prefix distributions differ.
statements.problem: The guarantee is overstated as applying at every position with only a positive base-recovery bound; the exact recovery solution is restricted to positions beyond the harm horizon and unrestricted distribution-space optimization.

statements.correction: The paper reports theoretical derivations and no trained-model evaluation of the recovery objective, robustness guarantee, or capability cost; Limitations leaves finite-capacity implementation and finite-training attainment open.
statements.problem: The lack of empirical validation is correct, but the paper does not explicitly state the quoted absence of training and evaluation.
